As of 220 AM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Confluent flow driven by departing high pressure to the 
southeast, and a stalled stationary boundary over the Great Lakes 
and south into the Mid-Atlantic will push showers through the region 
this morning into the early afternoon. Radar depicts a broad area of 
light to moderate showers extending from the St. Lawrence Valley 
into northeastern Ontario. This area of showers will ride along a 
stationary boundary into northern New York with good isentropic 
lift, before diving south into the Hudson Valley, following the 
synoptic flow of the departing area of high pressure. Stratiform 
rain is expected across much of northern New York and areas south of 
I-89 in Vermont. The Northeast Kingdom may be able to stay dry 
through much of the day today. Rainfall rates will be fairly light 
with a thin warm cloud depth, in association with decently dry mid 
levels. Rainfall may resemble light rain or drizzle intermittently 
between showers. Most of the more persistent shower activity should 
move south and east of the region by this afternoon, with just some 
lingering light showers. Trends have kept the better instability and 
thunder chances to our southwest in the quasi warm sector and along 
the stationary boundary. Rainfall amounts through this evening are 
expected to be less than half and inch with a quarter to a half an 
inch southwest of a line from Massena, NY to the Orange/Caledonia 
County border in Vermont. As showers depart this afternoon, low 
level moisture will linger, though mid levels will remain fairly 
dry. Thus, some drizzle may still linger into the overnight hours, 
particularly in eastern Vermont where damed cold air will reside 
under the approaching warm air from the west leading to further 
isentropic lift. While it will not be a total washout today, with 
likely breaks between showers, especially this afternoon, it will 
likely be dreary. With the added cloud cover temperatures today 
temperatures will struggle to get out of the 60s in our south and 
western regions, with some warmer temperatures on the northern edge 
of the shower activity near the International Border where mid 70s 
will be possible.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A more dynamic system will push into the area Wednesday 
into Wednesday night as the stationary boundary to our southwest, 
drifts northeast closer to our region. A surface low over the Great 
Lakes associated with a parent low in northeast Ontario will track 
east from eastern Ontario. Showers are expected to move into the St. 
Lawrence Valley by the early afternoon on Wednesday, though with 
limited instability due to likely convective blowoff preceding 
these showers. However by the mid to late afternoon models depict 
good elevated instability above an inversion layer which could help 
sustain some thunderstorm activity primarily in the later afternoon 
and evening hours in the St. Lawrence Valley. 1000-1500J/kg of 
MLCAPE associated with 30-40kts of 0-6km bulk shear would be ample 
to support embedded thunderstorms towards the later afternoon. Any 
stronger storms Wednesday afternoon, would be tied to northwestern 
New York, and conditional on the amount of cloud cover and 
antecedent convection. Temperature profiles likely will not be of 
much help with surface temperatures in the mid to upper 70s 
Wednesday afternoon. Should convection become self-sustaining in 
Canada, it likely would be able to continue due to the available 
MUCAPE to 1500-2000J/kg modeled across the St. Lawrence Valley. As a 
result of this slight upward trend, the Storm Prediction Center has 
added southwestern St. Lawrence County in a Marginal Risk (level 1 
out of 5) for Severe thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon-Wednesday 
night. As the showers and embedded thunderstorms continue to track 
east Wednesday evening, a developing nocturnal inversion will help 
decrease the threat of any stronger storms in addition to the 
overall thunder chances. However, showers will still retain the 
potential for heavier downpours into Vermont beyond sunset. Rainfall 
rates in the HREF through Wednesday evening denote pockets of 0.25-
0.5"/hour rates across northern New York. A good wetting rain is 
anticipated Wednesday night areawide with most areas expected to see 
three-quarters of an inch to an inch of rain, with perhaps an inch 
to 1.5 inches in the higher terrain of the Greens. Ensembles still 
show a 20-50% chance of receiving an inch or more, with 2 inch 
probabilities unchanged and less than 10%. While most of the area is 
still in a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) for the potential for 
isolated Flash Flooding, the threat remains low and conditional upon 
the heavy rain axis becoming colocated with the rain axis today.
